items.title: A phone ban in high schools
items.instructions: Read the following article from a local newspaper.

passage.title: School Board Considers Phone Ban
paragraphs: The Westbrook School Board will vote next month on a proposal to ban cellphones in all of its high schools during the school day. If the proposal passes, students would have to keep their phones in their lockers from the first bell until the end of classes, including at lunch.

Supporters say the ban would help students concentrate. Maria Lopez, a math teacher at Westbrook Central, says she spends the first ten minutes of many classes asking students to put their phones away. "Even when the phones are face down on the desk, students are thinking about them," she says. "I've seen grades improve in classes where phones are collected at the door." Supporters also point to a survey of local parents, in which 64 percent said they would welcome a ban, mainly because they believe it would reduce online bullying during school hours.

Others think the proposal goes too far. Student council president Jacob Martin argues that phones are useful learning tools. "We use them to look up information, take photos of the whiteboard and check our schedules," he says. Jacob suggests a compromise: phones could be banned during class time but allowed at lunch and between classes. Some parents are also worried about safety. They want to be able to contact their children in an emergency, especially those who take public transit to school.

School principal Diane Wong understands both sides. Her school tried a classroom-only ban last year, and teachers reported fewer distractions. However, she believes that students need to learn how to manage their phone use, not simply have their phones taken away. "In a few years, they'll be at university or at work, and no one will be collecting their phones," she says. She would prefer to combine classroom rules with lessons about healthy technology habits.
The board will hold a public meeting on May 14, where students, parents and teachers can share their views before the vote.

items.title: A four-day work week
items.instructions: Read the following article from a business magazine.

passage.title: A Shorter Week: Success or Illusion?
paragraphs: Last year, Clearwater Insurance, a company with 400 employees in Edmonton, tried something unusual. For six months, most staff worked four days a week instead of five, for the same pay. Employees worked eight hours a day, which meant a total of 32 hours a week instead of 40.

The company's chief executive, Sandra Patel, calls the trial a clear success. "We expected productivity to drop, but it actually rose by about five percent," she says. According to Patel, employees took fewer sick days, and the company received twice as many job applications as before. "People want to work here now. That alone saves us a lot of money in hiring costs."

Employees were mostly positive, but not all of them. Customer service manager Tom Becker says his team found the change difficult. "Our customers expect us to answer the phone five days a week," he explains. His team had to create a complicated schedule so that someone was always available, and some employees ended up working longer days during busy periods. "For office staff, the four-day week works. For people who deal with the public, it's not so simple."

Economist Rachel Nguyen, who studies working hours, is cautious about the results. She points out that the trial lasted only six months, and that employees may have worked harder because they wanted the program to continue. "The real question is whether these gains last after two or three years," she says. She also notes that the trial took place during a quiet period for the insurance industry.
Clearwater has decided to continue the four-day week for another year, with one change. Customer service staff will be able to choose between a four-day week and a five-day week with shorter days.

The trial was short and employees wanted it to continue.
questions.explanation: The trial lasted only six months, and employees may have worked harder to keep the program.

options: Let customer service staff choose their schedule

items.title: Bike lanes or parking?
items.instructions: Read the following article from a local newspaper.

passage.title: Bike Lanes or Parking? Downtown Debate Heats Up
paragraphs: The city of Lakeshore is planning to remove 120 parking spaces on Queen Street to build a protected bike lane. The plan, which would cost about $2 million, is part of the city's goal of doubling the number of people who cycle to work by 2032.

Cycling groups are delighted. "Right now, Queen Street is one of the most dangerous streets in the city for cyclists," says Priya Desai of Lakeshore Bikes. She notes that three cyclists were seriously injured on the street last year. Desai believes a protected lane, separated from traffic by a concrete curb, would encourage many people who are currently afraid to ride. "Lots of people would cycle if they felt safe. Paint on the road isn't enough."

Many business owners are worried. Luc Tremblay, who has owned a hardware store on Queen Street for 22 years, says most of his customers drive. "You can't carry a ladder or ten litres of paint on a bicycle," he says. Tremblay fears that customers will go to the big stores at the edge of the city, where parking is free. The local business association has asked the city to delay the project and study its effect on sales.

City planner Grace Liu says the city has considered these concerns. Studies from other cities, she explains, show that people who arrive on foot or by bike visit shops more often and spend more money over a month than drivers do. The city also plans to add 60 new parking spaces in a lot one block away and to create short-term loading zones for deliveries and for customers picking up large items.
City council will make a final decision in September. If the plan is approved, construction would begin next spring.
